clinicalPearls: A localised variant of pemphigus foliaceus that shows clinical and immunological overlap with lupus erythematosus; also known as Senear-Usher syndrome.
Presents with erythematous, scaly, crusted plaques and flaccid superficial blisters in a seborrhoeic and photodistributed pattern — malar 'butterfly' face, scalp and upper trunk.
The Nikolsky sign is typically positive, while mucosal involvement is characteristically absent (unlike pemphigus vulgaris).
Autoantibodies target desmoglein 1, producing superficial acantholysis in the granular/subcorneal layer identical to pemphigus foliaceus.
Direct immunofluorescence shows the hallmark dual pattern: intercellular ('chicken-wire') IgG and C3 within the epidermis PLUS granular IgG/C3 at the basement membrane zone.
Antinuclear antibodies are frequently positive, yet most patients do not fulfil criteria for true systemic lupus erythematosus.
Sunlight and thiol/sulfhydryl drugs (for example penicillamine or captopril) can precipitate or aggravate disease, so photoprotection matters.
Course is generally more benign and localised than pemphigus vulgaris, but it may occasionally evolve into generalised pemphigus foliaceus.
reference.pathophysiology: Pemphigus erythematosus is an autoimmune intraepidermal blistering disorder in which IgG autoantibodies are directed against desmoglein 1, a desmosomal cadherin expressed most abundantly in the superficial (granular) layer of the epidermis. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes, causing acantholysis high in the epidermis and the resulting fragile, superficial blisters and scaly crusted erosions. What distinguishes the entity from ordinary pemphigus foliaceus is a concurrent lupus-like immunological signature, including positive antinuclear antibodies and granular deposition of immunoglobulin and complement along the dermo-epidermal junction (a 'lupus band'), so it is regarded as an overlap of pemphigus foliaceus and cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Because desmoglein 1 predominates superficially and mucosae are protected by compensatory desmoglein 3, blistering is superficial and mucosal surfaces are typically spared. Ultraviolet light and thiol-containing or other implicated drugs can trigger or exacerbate the autoimmune response, and lesions favour sun-exposed, seborrhoeic sites.
additionalInvestigations: Lesional skin biopsy showing superficial acantholysis in the granular layer
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin demonstrating the combined intercellular and basement-membrane pattern
Indirect immunofluorescence for circulating intercellular (anti-desmoglein) antibodies
Antinuclear antibodies with extended lupus serology (anti-dsDNA, extractable nuclear antigens) and complement
Careful drug history for thiol/sulfhydryl-containing agents
Assessment for systemic lupus features (renal and haematological screening)
redFlags: Rapid extension to widespread erosions with skin-barrier failure and associated fluid and thermoregulatory compromise
Secondary bacterial infection or sepsis of eroded skin
Emergence of systemic lupus features such as renal impairment, cytopenias or serositis
reference.prognosis: Pemphigus erythematosus usually follows a chronic but comparatively benign and localised course, and generally responds to treatment. Relapses are common, and a minority progress to more generalised pemphigus foliaceus.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the eruption as seborrhoeic dermatitis or lupus and delaying diagnostic immunofluorescence.
Failing to recognise the combined intercellular plus basement-membrane immunofluorescence pattern that defines the entity.
Interpreting antinuclear antibody positivity as proof of systemic lupus erythematosus.
Overlooking a drug trigger, particularly thiol/sulfhydryl agents.
Neglecting photoprotection advice, allowing ultraviolet-driven flares.
